strengths: The paper identifies an important evaluation gap: typographic robustness and legitimate text reading are usually measured separately, allowing defenses that simply suppress text. Framing the desired capability as context-dependent selective text use is intuitive and relevant to real-world LVLM deployment.

Although no contribution type is explicitly declared, the work is best assessed as Datasets/Benchmarks rather than primarily as a new algorithm. Under that framing, the same-scene Object/Text × Clean/Attack structure is a useful contribution that enables more controlled analysis than combining unrelated object- and text-VQA datasets.

The benchmark construction is described in substantial detail, including dataset sizes, hierarchical negative sampling, rendering parameters, placement rules, prompts, metrics, and training configurations. The intended release of generation code and metadata should support reproducibility.

The empirical evaluation is broad: six LVLM configurations are tested on the main benchmark, with comparisons to pretrained models, a reproduced prompting defense, and an ignore-text training baseline. Results consistently expose the robustness/reading trade-off that motivates the work.

RIO-RT is simple but effective within the proposed setting. Balanced training greatly improves attacked Object-VQA while generally preserving or improving Text-VQA, whereas object-only robust training often damages reading ability.

Cross-dataset tests on Typo-D, AI2D, ChartQA, DocVQA, and InfoVQA materially strengthen the evidence. In several models, RIO-RT transfers typographic robustness while retaining substantially more text-reading ability than the ignore-text baseline.
The supplementary material provides useful construction details, qualitative examples, computational costs, LoRA-placement analysis, and a training-size ablation.
weaknesses: The benchmark lacks a reported human-validation study. Object labels are selected automatically using Open Images annotations and CLIP, text distractors are generated by an LLM, and key-text regions can fall back to the largest OCR box. The displayed examples themselves include questionable TextVQA pairs, such as asking what kind of beer appears in images of a baseball player or a watch. The paper should quantify label correctness, attack plausibility, answerability, and inter-annotator agreement on a representative sample.

The claimed same-scene counterfactual control is imperfect. In several supplementary examples, the multiple-choice option order changes between Obj-Clean and Obj-Attack, so the image overlay is not the only changed variable. Paired variants should use exactly the same question and option order to eliminate position-related confounds.

RIO-RT may learn synthetic-generation cues rather than a general notion of selective text use. Attacks use constrained fonts, colors, placement policies, and simple overlays, while the object attack word is explicitly one of the MC distractors. Nearly saturated in-domain attacked-MC accuracy is therefore not sufficient to establish semantic context-aware reasoning. More tests with unseen fonts/renderers, natural or physical adversarial text, alternative attack generators, and explicit style-held-out splits are needed.

The external results partially address distribution shift, but they do not isolate generalization to text attacks: Typo-D evaluates object-centric robustness, while the external text-centric datasets are reported only in clean form. The central claim would be stronger with attacked text-reading evaluation on independently constructed or naturally occurring data.

R-CLIP-M is insufficiently validated. It subtracts two binary top-5 retrieval indicators, can reward or penalize outputs in unintuitive ways, and is not shown to correlate with human judgments. Results should include metric distributions or confusion cases and comparisons with exact class extraction, semantic judges, or human evaluation.

The experimental uncertainty is not characterized. LoRA training, 16K-example sampling, option shuffling, and attack placement are stochastic, yet only single numbers are reported without repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This is especially relevant for small claimed clean-performance differences.

The attention-map analysis overstates mechanistic conclusions. Last-question-token attention ratios do not establish that the language model is performing contextual reasoning, and the evidence consists of a small number of selected examples. Claims such as robustness arising “only” from language-model reasoning are stronger than supported by the LoRA-placement ablation and attention visualization.

The comparison set remains limited: the only directly reproduced prior LVLM defense is CoT, while IT-RT is an author-created adaptation. Even if earlier CLIP defenses are not directly applicable, stronger generic alternatives—such as OCR-assisted filtering, instruction tuning with independent data, augmentation baselines, or explicit read/ignore routing—would better contextualize RIO-RT.

Dataset licensing, inherited demographic/content biases, risks from manipulated text, and safeguards for deployment-sensitive domains such as autonomous driving receive little discussion. These issues are particularly relevant for a benchmark presented as motivating real-world reliability.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and underexplored evaluation gap: typographic robustness should not be achieved by globally suppressing text sensitivity, because practical vision-language systems must sometimes read text and sometimes disregard it.

The same-scene construction is conceptually appealing. Pairing object- and text-centric questions with clean and attacked variants controls scene content better than evaluating robustness and reading ability on unrelated datasets.

RIO-Bench is reasonably large, covers multiple attack difficulty levels and both multiple-choice and open-ended questions, and is evaluated on six LVLMs. The appendix provides useful construction, training, metric, and computational details, with a commitment to release generation code.

The experiments clearly demonstrate the anticipated failure mode of ignore-text training: IT-RT substantially improves object robustness while often damaging TextVQA accuracy. This is a useful empirical warning for the field.

The external evaluation on Typo-D and four text-centric VQA datasets is valuable and provides some evidence that RIO-RT's gains are not entirely confined to the benchmark. The low training cost also makes the approach practically reproducible.
weaknesses: The paper is best assessed primarily as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution, despite also presenting a defense. Under that standard, the central weakness is insufficient validation that RIO-Bench measures semantic, context-dependent text selection rather than exploitable construction artifacts.

The benchmark makes the read/ignore decision unusually easy to infer from the question distribution. Object questions use one of two fixed templates, whereas text questions are inherited from TextVQA and are linguistically diverse. A model can therefore select a behavior from the prompt form alone, without reasoning about image context. The paper's claim that RIO-RT learns a genuinely new context-aware capability is consequently not established.

Synthetic attack text has conspicuous, restricted rendering styles, and train and validation examples follow the same generation procedure. The paper does not test held-out fonts, colors, rendering engines, placement policies, natural adversarial text, or physical attacks. Near-perfect in-benchmark object-attack accuracy after fine-tuning may therefore reflect detection of synthetic overlays rather than general typographic robustness.

Dataset quality control is inadequate. Text-attack words are generated automatically by Llama-3, while the supporting text region is found through heuristic OCR matching that can fall back to the largest OCR box. The manuscript reports neither human validation nor statistics for matching failures, invalid or non-contradictory distractors, ambiguous questions, and genuinely absent object negatives. Thus, the answerability and semantic validity of the benchmark are uncertain.

The proposed RIO-RT defense is essentially supervised fine-tuning on a balanced mixture of object-attack and text-attack samples. Its advantage over IT-RT follows directly from providing the latter no text-reading training data. There are no stronger controls such as ordinary mixed clean-task rehearsal, equal mixtures with alternative augmentations, or curriculum/multitask baselines, so the evidence does not isolate what is novel or necessary about RIO-RT.

The baseline comparison is narrow: only one inference-time CoT defense and the authors' constructed IT-RT baseline are evaluated. The claim of moving beyond existing defenses is therefore broader than the direct evidence, even if some prior CLIP-specific methods are not immediately applicable.

The external results are mixed and undercut the broad claim of preserved text understanding. For example, RIO-RT lowers average external text-VQA performance for LLaVA-1.5-13B and slightly for Qwen2.5-VL-7B, while improvements vary greatly by model. No external benchmark jointly tests reading and ignoring under matched natural scenes.

Results are presented without confidence intervals, repeated training runs, significance tests, or sensitivity to random attack placement and sampled training examples. This is particularly problematic because the construction and training contain several random choices.

The open-ended object evaluation introduces R-CLIP-M, a coarse difference of two top-5 binary retrieval indicators. The paper provides no validation that this metric agrees with human judgments, no sensitivity analysis for k, and limited explanation of how negative values and clean cases are summarized. Conclusions drawn from these scores are therefore less secure.

The attention-map discussion makes mechanistic claims from a single qualitative example and selected layers. Attention does not by itself demonstrate reasoning, and no aggregate localization analysis supports statements that the model learned contextual prioritization.

Overall, the core problem formulation is worthwhile, but benchmark shortcuts, absent human quality validation, limited controls, and overstated claims prevent a convincing scientific case in the current version. These are consequential issues rather than minor presentation corrections.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and underexplored failure mode: robustness obtained by suppressing all image text is incompatible with applications that must selectively use relevant text. The Read-or-Ignore formulation is intuitive and practically motivated.

Although no contribution type is explicitly declared, the work is best assessed as Datasets/Benchmarks rather than primarily as a new algorithm. Under that framing, the same-scene Object/Text × Clean/Attack design is a meaningful contribution because it exposes a trade-off hidden by conventional object-only robustness evaluations.

The empirical study is broad, covering six LVLMs of different architectures and sizes. Table 1 shows a consistent pattern: pretrained models are vulnerable, while object-only robust training improves attack performance at substantial cost to text reading.

RIO-RT is simple but effective. Balanced training produces large in-domain robustness gains while generally preserving or improving text-VQA performance, strongly supporting the paper's central hypothesis that training data must include both read and ignore cases.

The evaluation goes beyond the proposed benchmark: results on Typo-D and four text-centric VQA datasets provide useful evidence of cross-domain transfer. Ablations on attack difficulty, LoRA placement, and training-set size further strengthen the study.

The benchmark construction, evaluation metrics, training recipe, computational cost, prompts, and dataset statistics are described in considerable detail, and the authors commit to releasing generation code.
weaknesses: The most important concern is insufficient validation of benchmark quality. There is no reported human audit of object labels, generated contradictory phrases, key-text localization, attack feasibility, or question-answer consistency. This is especially concerning because Figures 9–11 contain visibly mismatched TextVQA examples—for instance, a watch and a whiteboard are paired with the question “what kind of beer is this?” and incompatible answers. The paper must clarify whether this is only a figure-generation error or reflects dataset misalignment, and should report a statistically meaningful manual-quality study.

The very strong in-domain RIO-RT results may partly reflect generator-specific shortcuts. Attacks use standardized fonts, rendering rules, placements, and difficulty construction, and training and validation share this synthetic pipeline. The external experiments establish transfer of object robustness and preservation of ordinary text reading, but they do not test selective reading under independently generated text attacks, unseen typography, physical attacks, or another read/ignore benchmark.

The claim that RIO-RT learns “genuine” contextual reasoning is stronger than the evidence. Question type itself clearly signals whether text should be used, and the attention visualization consists of one example; attention patterns do not establish the proposed causal mechanism. Testing paraphrased or ambiguous questions, conflicting multimodal evidence, and explicit shortcut controls would better support this interpretation.

The Object-OE evaluation relies on the proposed R-CLIP-M difference of two binary top-5 retrieval indicators. Its calibration and correlation with human judgments are not validated, and semantically related ground-truth and attack classes could both enter the top five, producing unintuitive scores. Human evaluation or comparison against alternative semantic metrics is needed.

Baseline coverage is limited. CoT is the only prior LVLM defense, while IT-RT is constructed by the authors. Even if CLIP-specific defenses cannot be directly applied, simple competitive controls—explicit read/ignore prompting, OCR-assisted reasoning, text masking, or matched multitask fine-tuning without attacks—would help isolate the benefit of the proposed construction.

Results are apparently from single fine-tuning runs, with no variance, uncertainty estimates, or significance analysis. Additional presentation inconsistencies also need correction, including Qwen3-VL being described as 8B in the setup but labeled 7B in Table 1, and the incomplete project-page statement in the abstract.

The limitations discussion is too narrow for a benchmark paper: it mentions only the restriction to VQA, omitting synthetic-attack realism, dependence on TextVQA/Open Images annotations, English-centric evaluation, potential label noise, and the possibility that conspicuous overlays favor shortcut learning. These issues make the case a borderline rather than clear acceptance despite the promising core contribution.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and underexplored failure mode: typographic robustness obtained by suppressing all textual evidence is unsuitable for applications that must also read relevant scene text. The read-or-ignore framing is intuitive and potentially useful to the vision-language community.

Although no contribution type is explicitly declared, the work is best assessed as Datasets/Benchmarks rather than Algorithms/General because its primary contribution is RIO-Bench; under that framing, the controlled crossing of question intent and text condition on shared source images is a meaningful contribution.

The evaluation is broad: RIO-Bench contains 3,166 validation scenes and multiple object/text, clean/attack, MC/OE, difficulty, and rendering conditions. Experiments cover six primary LVLMs, additional recent and frontier models, controlled overlays, and more realistic SceneTAP insertions.

The human audit is valuable. Across four strata, 95.5–97.5% of audited samples receive majority-desirable judgments, with high reported inter-rater agreement. This directly addresses concerns arising from automated question and attack generation.

RIO-RT is a simple but effective reference baseline. Its comparison with object-only IT-RT clearly illustrates the benchmark's intended trade-off, while transfer to unseen SceneTAP attacks, Typo-D, and external text-VQA datasets provides evidence beyond the training distribution.

Construction prompts, hierarchy-based sampling, attack parameters, training hyperparameters, computational costs, and the reproduced CoT prompt are documented in considerable detail. The paper is generally clear, well organized, and appropriately acknowledges its restricted VQA and threat-model scope.
weaknesses: The central claim that counterfactual pairs vary only text condition is not strictly satisfied. In the appendix examples, multiple-choice option order—and consequently the correct answer letter—changes between Obj-Clean and Obj-Attack. SceneTAP also uses diffusion editing that can modify non-text pixels. These changes introduce avoidable confounds into paired comparisons and should be removed or quantitatively bounded.

Some instances are epistemically ambiguous: when a scene-coherent insertion supplies a second plausible answer, the model has no access to the construction-time fact that one text string is original and the other is a distractor. Thus, success can sometimes require detecting synthetic provenance rather than context-dependent relevance. The audit mitigates this concern, but only 100 examples per stratum were assessed and the paper does not analyze ambiguity by attack type or difficulty.

The proposed R-CLIP-M metric needs stronger validation. Subtracting attack-word top-K retrieval from ground-truth top-K retrieval yields a nonstandard score that can be negative, depends on an arbitrary K=5 and CLIP's semantic geometry, and may treat multi-object predictions unexpectedly. The manuscript is also unclear about handling the multiple acceptable OE object labels described in the appendix. Human correlation, K-sensitivity, and comparison with alternative semantic metrics are needed.

The largest RIO-RT gains are measured on the same benchmark-generation pipeline used for training. Transfer to SceneTAP and Typo-D is encouraging, but the external text-VQA evaluation contains no paired attacks and therefore does not establish out-of-domain read-or-ignore behavior. Evaluation on another independently constructed or physical attack dataset would materially strengthen the scientific case.

The evidence for broad claims about existing defenses is limited: CoT is the only directly reproduced prior LVLM defense, while IT-RT is the authors' own adaptation. Comparisons with simple OCR masking, explicit OCR-plus-routing, text-region filtering, or other selective-text baselines would clarify whether RIO-RT learns the intended capability rather than overlay-specific rejection cues.

Several mechanistic interpretations are overstated. Language-only LoRA performance does not establish that selective behavior is governed by language-model 'reasoning,' and attention ratios from the last question token—illustrated with essentially one case—are not causal evidence that the model selectively disregards distractors.

For a benchmark contribution, artifact availability is important, yet the manuscript gives no concrete dataset/code release location or licensing/distribution statement. Random seeds, decoding settings, preprocessing details, and exact proprietary-model configurations are also insufficiently specified for complete reproduction.

strengths: Although no contribution type is explicitly declared, the work is best assessed as Datasets/Benchmarks rather than Algorithms/General. Under that framing, jointly measuring when models should read versus ignore image text is a relevant and practically motivated problem. RIO-Bench has useful breadth: 3,166 validation scenes, object- and text-centric questions, controlled overlays, SceneTAP insertions, multiple difficulty levels, and both multiple-choice and open-ended evaluation.

The empirical study covers six principal LVLMs, additional modern/frontier models, inference- and training-time baselines, parameter-placement and data-size ablations, and transfer to Typo-D and four text-centric VQA datasets.

The comparison between IT-RT and RIO-RT clearly illustrates the intended diagnostic: object-only adversarial training can substantially damage scene-text performance, whereas balanced training usually preserves it. A three-annotator audit also provides some evidence that automatically constructed samples remain answerable.
weaknesses: The claimed same-scene counterfactual control is not actually maintained for multiple-choice examples. Figures 6–11 show that clean and attacked instances reshuffle the answer options, changing both the question string and correct option letter in addition to modifying the image. Consequently, paired prediction changes cannot be attributed solely to inserted text. This directly undermines the benchmark's central methodological claim, even if randomization may average out in aggregate accuracy.

The broad conclusion that prevailing defenses achieve robustness by suppressing text is supported mainly by one reproduced CoT prompt explicitly instructing models to de-emphasize text and by IT-RT, an intentionally object-only baseline designed by the authors. Most cited defenses are declared inapplicable and are not tested. This evidence demonstrates that one-sided training can induce the trade-off, but not the repeatedly claimed fundamental misalignment of existing defenses as a class.

The proposed R-CLIP-M metric is insufficiently validated. It subtracts two top-K binary retrieval scores, can take negative values, depends on CLIP both for selecting object ground truth and evaluating predictions, and has no reported correlation with human judgments or conventional semantic-answer metrics. The manuscript is also unclear about how the attack-word penalty applies to clean samples and how multiple valid Open Images labels are reconciled with the singular ground-truth formulation.

Object questions are synthetic and unusually constrained: every MC question uses the same presence template, the positive is selected using CLIP, and the inserted word is literally one of the answer choices. Clean accuracies around 92–98% indicate that this is often a trivial presence task, while the attack setting strongly rewards resisting an explicit lexical copy shortcut. It is therefore uncertain whether results generalize to natural object reasoning or genuinely context-dependent read/ignore decisions.

RIO-RT is straightforward supervised fine-tuning on examples produced by the benchmark's own attack generator. Its near-perfect object-attack results are difficult to separate from learning generator-specific cues. SceneTAP reuses the same attack words, and the external evaluation does not test unseen text-attack generators; external text-reading transfer is also mixed, including an 8% average decline for LLaVA-1.5-13B in Table 7.

Important construction failure rates are omitted, including how often key-text matching falls back to the largest OCR box, how often SceneTAP reaches relaxed or forced-placement fallbacks, and how often OCR misses existing text that an overlay may occlude. The 400-sample audit is helpful but too small and coarsely reported to characterize these pipeline-specific errors across 34,826 evaluation instances.

Overall, the benchmark idea and experimental effort have merit, but the broken MC counterfactual control, unvalidated custom metric, and overextended defense claims leave the central scientific case insufficiently convincing in its current form. These concerns favor a borderline rejection rather than an outright reject because the underlying benchmark concept could become valuable after reconstruction and stronger validation.

strengths: Although no contribution type is explicitly declared, the paper is best assessed as Datasets/Benchmarks: its central contribution is RIO-Bench and the RIO-VQA evaluation protocol, while RIO-RT is appropriately presented as a reference baseline rather than a novel algorithm. Under this framing, the work makes a clear and practically important contribution.

The paper identifies a genuine blind spot in typographic-attack evaluation: a defense can appear robust on object-centric tasks merely by suppressing text sensitivity, even though real applications may require reading relevant scene text. The read-or-ignore formulation captures this tension clearly.

The same-scene design is thoughtful. Pairing object- and text-centric questions on the same TextVQA/Open Images scenes and constructing clean/attacked counterparts reduces scene-level confounding and enables direct behavioral comparisons.

The benchmark is reasonably broad and carefully constructed: it includes multiple-choice and open-ended object VQA, text VQA, semantic and spatial attack difficulty levels, controlled overlays, and scene-coherent SceneTAP insertions. OCR-aware placement helps avoid corrupting answer-bearing text.

The empirical evaluation is extensive, covering six varied LVLM backbones for defense comparisons, additional modern and frontier models, model scaling, LoRA placement, attack difficulty, attention visualizations, and training-data size.

The main empirical finding is consistent and useful: object-only robust training substantially improves attack robustness but can severely damage text reading, whereas balanced RIO-RT usually improves robustness while preserving or improving text-dependent performance. For example, on LLaVA-1.5-7B, RIO-RT raises average MC attack accuracy from 71.6 to 98.2 while increasing Text-Clean from 49.5 to 53.3, unlike IT-RT, which reduces Text-Clean to 30.3.

Evidence extends beyond the most favorable in-distribution setting. RIO-RT is trained only on overlay attacks but transfers to SceneTAP, Typo-D, and several external text-centric VQA benchmarks, although the strength of transfer varies by model.

The 400-sample stratified human audit reports high desirable rates (95.5–97.5%) and strong agreement (Gwet's AC1 of 0.89–0.94), providing useful validation of an otherwise largely automated construction pipeline. Construction details, prompts, metrics, training settings, and computational costs are also documented well.
weaknesses: The evaluation remains narrower than the motivating real-world claims. Most samples come from one source dataset, overlays use a single font and limited rendering policy, and the realistic condition uses one generative insertion pipeline. Physical attacks, multilingual text, handwritten or stylized typography, adaptive attackers, and embodied decision tasks are not evaluated.

RIO-RT's strongest results are obtained on data produced by the same benchmark-generation process used for training. SceneTAP transfer is encouraging, but it reuses the same distractor words and TextVQA scenes. Thus, near-saturated object-attack results may partly reflect benchmark-specific adaptation rather than a general solution to selective text use.

The proposed R-CLIP-M metric needs stronger validation. Subtracting attack-word retrieval from ground-truth retrieval is intuitive but can produce a score whose interpretation differs from ordinary accuracy, depends on CLIP's semantic geometry and the chosen top-K, and may penalize an otherwise correct multi-object answer that truthfully mentions both concepts. Correlation with human judgments and sensitivity to K or the embedding model are not reported.

The object-question construction is partly circular with respect to CLIP: CLIP selects the ground-truth class from Open Images annotations, and a CLIP-based metric evaluates open-ended answers. This may introduce model-dependent label bias, while the generic question 'What objects can be seen' can have several valid answers beyond the selected labels.

The paper reports point estimates only. There are no multiple training seeds, confidence intervals, or significance analyses, despite some preservation/generalization differences being small and LoRA fine-tuning potentially variable.

The attention visualization supports intuition but is based on a single qualitative example and last-question-token attention ratios. It is insufficient to substantiate the stronger mechanistic claim that selective behavior is primarily governed by language-side reasoning; the parameter-placement ablation supports that claim only behaviorally.

Reproducibility is good at the methodological level but incomplete operationally: the manuscript does not clearly provide a benchmark/code release URL, random seeds, complete inference settings for every model, or precise snapshots/configurations for proprietary frontier models. Dataset redistribution and licensing details for the derived TextVQA/Open Images and generated assets should also be made explicit.
